title: Back to the river bank
body: Which parts of this prefix would help you choose a continuation?

title: One head can read the setting
body: In this hand-chosen two-head example, the first head gives river a large weight. Its values carry setting information to the receiver.

title: Another head can read who is there
body: The sentence and receiver stay fixed. A different head gives fisherman a large weight.

title: One head shares one set of source weights
body: A single head can mix many words. But every coordinate of its message uses the same attention-weight row.

title: Keep both readings
body: Two heads can retain different source mixtures at the same token. They run in parallel, not one after the other.

title: How do we make the readings different?
Give both heads the same input
body: We will zoom into these two branches. Each starts with the same embedding rows and sends back its own message.

title: The same embedding makes two queries
body: Both heads read all four input coordinates. Superscripts label the heads. We choose two query/key coordinates per head here; Part II’s toy used three.

title: Each query meets keys from its own head
body: Head 1 exposes water and finance in its keys. Head 2 exposes person and glue. Score every source with the matching query.

title: Each head gets its own weight row
body: Softmax runs across source positions, separately for each head. As before, \(\alpha_{ij}\) is one weight and \(A\) is the whole weight matrix.

title: Values turn those weights into messages
body: Keys set the weights; values carry the content. Here we chose equal key/value numbers, but their learned projections are separate.

title: What reaches the receiving token?
Put the messages side by side
body: Concatenation keeps the two messages separate. It does not add them coordinate by coordinate.

title: Map the messages back to embedding space
body: \(W_O\) learns how the head messages contribute to the embedding update. Four joined coordinates become four update coordinates.

title: Add context to the original embedding
body: Exactly as in Part II: \(e_i\) is the input embedding row, \(\Delta e_i\) is the context update, and \(e_i^{\prime}=e_i+\Delta e_i\).

title: Return to the next-token prediction
body: The last updated row still feeds the prediction MLP. More heads change how it reads context—not what the target means.

title: Try the other bank
Can every token do this at once?
Project every row with the same head matrix
body: Ten input rows × four coordinates. Multiplying by a 4 × 2 projection gives ten query rows × two coordinates.

title: One head makes one attention grid
body: Keep Part II’s notation: \(M\) is the causal mask, \(A=\operatorname{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}+M)\), and \(H=AV\) stores the message rows.

title: Two heads make two attention grids
body: Both heads receive the same E. Each uses its own projections, attention grid and values. Neither reads the other head’s output.

title: Join coordinates, not token rows
body: \(\Delta E=\operatorname{Concat}(H^{(1)},H^{(2)})W_O\), then \(E^{\prime}=E+\Delta E\). The superscript labels the head; each matrix still has ten token rows.

title: One head is still the Part II calculation
body: No new attention rule is needed. We reuse the same calculation with different learned matrices.
code:
def head(E, W_Q, W_K, W_V):
    Q, K, V = E @ W_Q, E @ W_K, E @ W_V
    scores = Q @ K.T / math.sqrt(Q.shape[-1])
    future = torch.ones(len(E), len(E), dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)
    A = scores.masked_fill(future, -torch.inf).softmax(-1)
    return A @ V

title: Call it with two sets of parameters
body: This unbatched example keeps one row per token. The notebook checks these outputs against the printed numbers.
code:
H1 = head(E, W_Q1, W_K1, W_V1)
H2 = head(E, W_Q2, W_K2, W_V2)
joined = torch.cat([H1, H2], dim=-1)  # [10, 4]
delta_E = joined @ W_O
E_prime = E + delta_E

title: The same loss trains both heads
body: Next-token cross-entropy trains all the projections together. We do not label training examples “setting head” or “person head”.

title: PyTorch packages the head calculation
body: Here E has shape [10, 4]: one unbatched sequence. PyTorch handles the projections and mixing. A contains two 10 × 10 weight grids.
code:
mha = nn.MultiheadAttention(embed_dim=4, num_heads=2, bias=False)
future = torch.ones(10, 10, dtype=torch.bool).triu(1)
delta_E, A = mha(E, E, E, attn_mask=future,
                 average_attn_weights=False)
E_prime = E + delta_E

title: Keep the total width fixed
body: The trained comparison uses width 64. Four smaller heads give four attention patterns with the same attention parameter count as one wide head.

title: Compare held-out next-token prediction
body: For each run, perplexity = exp(cross-entropy using natural logs). Lower means higher probability for observed tokens. The table averages three seeds on the same test stories.

title: Compare size and training time too
body: Mean training times on Apple M2 Max/MPS, including validation. The two attention models have equal parameter counts; four heads took slightly longer.
